newsitem.title: USA: Most IMM currencies end lower on positive dlr talk.
newsitem.headline: Most IMM currencies end lower on positive dlr talk.

text.p: Most IMM currency futures closed lower, as the U.S. dollar rose to the upper end of its recent ranges after German central bankers spoke positively about the U.S. currency, traders and analysts said.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer comments that the U.S. dollar was once again on its way back up and that he welcomed the dollar being at its correct level was the latest in dollar-supportive statements from Bundesbank officials.
Comments from Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp and Bundesbank directorate member Edgar Meister supported the dollar earlier in the day.
However, Tietmeyer's statements sparked heavy fund selling in the pits, traders said. Analysts also said the selling was inspired by expectations for favorable U.S. inflation data this week.

"The Bundesbank came out with stronger dollar comments, and people are anticipating numbers that will be more or less kind to the marketplace," Pat Donahue, head of the forex desk at Nationsbanc, said.
The U.S. October Producer Price Index (PPI) and Consumer Price Index (CPI) are forecast to rise slightly in both its overall and core rates from September.
In addition, a U.S. official said on Tuesday U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin and Japanese finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka did not dicuss forex rates in a telephone call.
The official, who said Rubin was on vacation in the latter half of last week, said Rubin and Mitsuzuka did discuss financial services, including Japan's insurance market.
One large bank sold about 2,000 December yen at $0.009010 to $0.009000, pushing the contract to $0.008983, which roughly corresponds to the dollar/yen's high of 111.80 spot yen.
However, the rise in the dollar merely put the U.S. currency in the upper end of its recent ranges.
December yen still remained above Monday's GLOBEX low of $0.008973.
While December marks did edge below Monday's overall low of $0.6658, the contract found support at $0.6637, well-above the three-week low of $0.6566, or 1.5245 spot.
Donahue said central banks around the world were probably attempting to stabilize the U.S. dollar within ranges.

"For the rest of the year, central banks are going to be attempting to lock dollar/mark between 1.4850 and 1.52," he said. The 1.4850 to 1.520 spot range is equivalent to $0.6749 to $0.6593 in December marks.

At the end of pit trade, December yen was off $0.000047 at $0.009006, marks were off $0.0067 at $0.6643, Swiss francs were $0.0081 lower at $0.7909, sterling was off $0.0018 at $1.6448, Canadian dollars were $0.0009 higher at $0.7521, Australian dollars were $0.0016 higher at $0.7872 and Mexican pesos were $0.000125 lower at $0.123325. -Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com
